scope: Pre-PR catalog categorization, naming and index review of the 92 new candidates and directly related existing categories. Includes regression and browser verification of the mixed parent/subsection area renderer.

summary.before: What a standard Gaussian matrix does: invariance, moments, inverse moments of the pseudoinverse, extreme singular values. The bottleneck for every Gaussian-sketch argument.
summary.after: Matrix-valued random models: Gaussian laws and inverse moments, spectral bounds, covariance, matrix chaos, Gaussian comparison and spectral universality.
Spectral norm, extreme eigenvalue and singular-value estimates, including lower bounds for sample covariance matrices.

name.after: Extreme eigenvalues, singular values and covariance

summary.before: Scalar and matrix tail bounds. The matrix side is done (Tropp Ch. 3–8); the scalar side is scattered across Mathlib and external libraries.
summary.after: Scalar and matrix probability bounds, Gaussian and exchangeable-pair identities, moment-generating functions, independence and martingales. Deterministic matrix-function theory lives under Matrix.
Importance sampling, leverage scores, determinant-weighted subsets, L-ensembles and their exact sampling and moment identities.

name.after: Leverage scores, volume sampling and determinantal laws

summary.before: Neumann series and inverse perturbation, condition numbers, forward-error bounds for linear systems and least squares, Cholesky and QR as existence-and-uniqueness statements.
summary.after: Inverse perturbation and condition numbers, forward-error bounds for linear systems and least squares, and reduced-Hessian solvability of constrained systems.

summary.before: Finite-dimensional deterministic regularization identities, stability bounds, and filtered pseudoinverses.
summary.after: Ordinary and total least squares, spectral regularization and filtered pseudoinverses, and nearest positive-semidefinite matrices.

name.before: Regularized least squares and spectral filters
name.after: Least squares, regularization and matrix nearness

summary.before: Fréchet derivatives, divided differences, positive-map inequalities and positive-definite matrix means.
summary.after: Functional calculus, Fréchet derivatives and divided differences, positive maps and matrix means, sign and polar iterations, and trace-exponential representations.
Solvability, separation, stability and residuals of finite matrix equations, with ADI and doubling recurrences. Projection methods remain under Krylov.
Gaussian proxies with matching full covariance, extreme-eigenvalue comparisons and resolvent-trace universality for independent matrix sums.

notes.before: Checked by CL^dagger C^T = C C^dagger, the Penrose identities and the trace/rank of a projector. The kernel of L consists of vectors constant on each connected component, proving the n-c extension of the source connected-graph n-1 formula. Orientation signs cancel. Resistance is asserted only for pairs joined by an edge (or, in a later extension, within one component): the pseudoinverse quadratic form is not the infinite electrical resistance across distinct components. Reuse Mathlib graph/incidence notions where available; weighted incidence and the physical-resistance bridge are prerequisites.
notes.after: Checked by CL^dagger C^T = C C^dagger, the Penrose identities and the trace/rank of a projector. The kernel of L consists of vectors constant on each connected component, proving the n-c extension of the source connected-graph n-1 formula. Orientation signs cancel. Resistance is asserted only for pairs joined by an edge (or, in a later extension, within one component): the pseudoinverse quadratic form is not the infinite electrical resistance across distinct components. Reuse Mathlib graph/incidence notions where available; weighted incidence and the physical-resistance bridge are prerequisites. The deterministic statement uses projector diagonals and rank, so it belongs in Matrix without importing Sketching. A bridge to the named leverage-score API belongs downstream in Sketching/Sampling.

conclusion.before: A well-defined unitarily equivariant rectangular spectral shrinkage map, with singular-value soft thresholding as a specialization.
conclusion.after: A well-defined unitarily equivariant rectangular singular-value transform, with singular-value soft thresholding as a specialization.

title.before: Singular-value shrinkage maps and independence of the chosen SVD
title.after: Singular-value transforms and independence of the chosen SVD

notes.before: Proof audit: telescope A^s X−X B^s, expand p(z)q(w)−q(z)p(w), and collect columns in span{M,AM,…,A^{k−1}M}. This yields νk, not the weaker νk² obtained by bounding every term separately. Multiplication by invertible q(A) and p(B) preserves rank. Writing the right factor as q(B)p(B)^{-1} permits poles of p/q on the B side; q(B) need not be invertible.
notes.after: Proof audit: telescope A^s X−X B^s, expand p(z)q(w)−q(z)p(w), and collect columns in span{M,AM,…,A^{k−1}M}. This yields νk, not the weaker νk² obtained by bounding every term separately. Multiplication by invertible q(A) and p(B) preserves rank. Writing the right factor as q(B)p(B)^{-1} permits poles of p/q on the B side; q(B) need not be invertible. The proof uses the span and rank of a concatenated matrix of columns M, AM, ..., A^(k-1)M; no import of the higher-layer Krylov API is required.

title.before: Inverse Gram and covariance identities under row-volume sampling
title.after: Inverse Gram and covariance bounds under row-volume sampling

informal.before: The inverse Gram matrix of a determinant-weighted row subset has an explicit Loewner upper bound, with equality exactly under an appropriate support hypothesis.
informal.after: The inverse Gram matrix of a determinant-weighted row subset has an explicit Loewner upper bound, with equality under full support.

notes.before: Proof audit for one right-hand side y: for a supported S and j outside S, det(X_S*X_S)|x_j*X_S^−1y_S−y_j|²=det([X,y]_(S+j)*[X,y]_(S+j)). Sum by T=S+j. Each (d+1)-row T is counted at most d+1 times, exactly d+1 under general position. Cauchy–Binet and det([X,y]*[X,y])=det(X*X)|| (I−P_X)y||² finish the bound. Sum over columns for Y; arbitrary y and Hermitian quadratic-form separation give the operator statement. The operator product is (I−H_S)*(I−H_S), not (I−H_S)^2: H_S is generally oblique. Exact-fit data and n=d give zero loss. Counterexample to unrestricted equality: X=[1;0], y=[0;1] gives expected loss 1, whereas (d+1) optimum loss is 2. This corrects the overstatement in Theorem 3.2 of 2510.02513v2.

notes.before: Independent realization proof: write M_t=(I−Π_t)Q* where Π_t projects onto the t selected columns of Q*. Because Q*Q=I_k, M_tM_t*=I−Π_t has trace k−t, so the displayed probabilities normalize and a positive pivot raises rank by one. Gram–Schmidt determinant multiplication gives the ordered path probability |det Q_S|²/k!; all k! orders of a nonsingular S are supported, giving the projection-DPP law. Apply the audited row-volume expectation/risk formulas columnwise. Zero leverage rows are never selected. The source states unconditional equality in its regression and interpolation formulas; the counterexample Q=[1;0], A=[0;1] disproves that. The inequality here is valid for every orthonormal Q; general position restores equality. The greedy pivoting rule on an arbitrary matrix is not claimed to sample its volume law.
